items: 1Know the origin of elements — how the Big Bang, stellar fusion, and artificial synthesis each contributed atoms to the universe.
2Identify the elements that constitute cells — the major, minor and trace elements, and why each is present (or excluded).
3Know why carbon is unique in its ability to form the enormous variety of compounds that build living matter.

blocks.x: Living cell An active cell that contains organised structures responsible for its function.
Element A substance whose atoms all have the same number of protons (the same atomic number).
Cells are viewed as the building blocks of an organism — but in biochemistry, it is the atoms and elements that are the true building blocks beneath them.
Atom→ Molecule→ Cell→ Tissue→ Organ→ Organ system→ Organism
Percentage distribution of elements in the human body
Trace elements (each <1.0%): B, Cr, Co, Cu, F, I, Fe, Mn, Mo, Se, Si, Sn, V, Zn.
Elements are believed to form through three processes: the Big Bang, fusion reactions inside stars, and artificial (laboratory) synthesis.

An explosion of an infinitely hot, dense ball of primordial matter occurred billions of years ago. Only hydrogen and helium formed in its immediate aftermath — no stars or light existed yet. Gravitational forces later drew clouds of this gas together, collapsing them into the vast galaxies of stars we see today.
The seven stages of the Big Bang

110⁻⁴³ secSuperfast "inflation" — the cosmos expands from atom-size to grapefruit-size. 210⁻³² secPost-inflation: a seething hot soup of electrons, quarks and other particles. 310⁻⁶ secRapid cooling permits quarks to clump into protons and neutrons. 43 minStill too hot for atoms; charged particles prevent light from shining — a superhot fog. 5300,000 yrsElectrons combine with protons/neutrons to form atoms (mostly H, He). Light can finally shine. 61 billion yrsGravity coalesces H and He gas into giant clouds — the first galaxies and stars. 715 billion yrsPresent day: galaxies cluster under gravity; dying stars spew heavy elements into space.
Further viewing: Origin of the Universe 101, National Geographic Channel.

All elements other than H and He formed in the centre of stars and were released upon their explosion. The Stellar hypothesis holds that very high temperatures and high concentrations of reactants are required — the temperature overcomes the electrostatic repulsion between positively charged nuclei that must fuse. Helium fusion (twice hydrogen's charge) needs roughly 20 × 10⁶ K.

blocks.title: Stellar hypothesis: from yellow star to supernova

blocks.x: Iron (Fe) is the largest atom formed directly by fusion. Heavier elements form only when Fe nuclei capture neutrons released during a star's explosion.
Oddo-Harkins rule: elements with even atomic numbers are far more abundant than odd-mass-numbered ones — except H and Be.

New elements with atomic numbers beyond 92 — the transuranium elements — are synthesised in the lab through fusion reactions. High-energy particles are accelerated in cyclotrons and fused with target nuclei.
Example: Seaborg et al. (1950) formed californium by firing helium nuclei (alpha particles) at curium-242 in a cyclotron.
About 32 elements are recognised as essential to cells — some in bulk, others only in trace amounts, and some deliberately excluded by nature.
Over 99% of the mass of most cells: C, H, O, N, P, S. Carbon is the most versatile and predominant element in the cell. Found mainly in the organic compounds of the cell.
Na, Mg, Ca, B, V, Mo, Mn, Fe, Co, Ni, Cu, Zn, Si, Se, Cl, Cr, I. Found mainly in the fluids that bathe the cells.

blocks.title: Notable features of the major elements

items: Neither too reactive nor too inert (unreactive)

blocks.x: Functions of minerals in the body

Earth's crust composition mirrors the body: O (48.9%), Fe (18.8%), Si (14.0%), Mg (12.4%), C (0.10%). Seawater and blood plasma share similar primary-ion concentrations (Cu²⁺, Mg²⁺, Ca²⁺, Na⁺, K⁺) — evidence that "man has his ancestry from the sea."
Almost every group of the periodic table has a representative in living cells — 15 of 18 groups. Except for the f-block (lanthanides/actinides), the s, p and d blocks all have representatives.
Elements beyond atomic number 92 (Tc, At, Fr) are man-made. Rare gases (He, Ne, Ar, Kr, Xe) and scarce lanthanides/actinides are excluded for being inert/unreactive.

Pb²⁺ inhibits haem synthesis (anaemia); Hg damages liver, kidney, brain; Be²⁺ interferes with Mg²⁺. Uranium's radioactivity harms cells — though some radioactive/toxic elements have medical value (Pt: anti-cancer; Au: anti-arthritis; Li₂CO₃: schizophrenia treatment; kaolin/Al: anti-diarrhoeal).
Carbon is the backbone of biological chemistry. Four properties explain why it — and almost nothing else — can build the molecular diversity of life.
Neither too small nor too big, so carbon forms stable covalent bonds.
The power to bond with itself in straight chains, branches, or rings.
Forms single, double or triple bonds with itself or other elements — a huge variety of organic compounds.
Carbon forms four bonds, maximising the structures it can build.

c: Ideal size + catenation + multiple bonds + tetravalency → maximum stable diversity.
Congener of carbon, but larger atomic size weakens Si–Si bonds (poor orbital overlap).
A lone pair remains after bonding; lone-pair repulsion lowers N–N bond energy.
